title: 22. Interview: Long Polling
summary: Interview Q&A for Long Polling — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Long Polling interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is long polling, and how does it differ from short polling?
**Answer:** Short polling: the client sends GET `/messages` every N seconds (say 5s); the server responds immediately with whatever is queued (possibly empty); the client waits 5s and asks again. Median latency to receive a new message is N/2 (2.5s on average for a 5s poll), and the client burns one HTTP request every N seconds even when nothing is happening — at 1M users × 1 req/5s = 200k requests/second of pure overhead. Long polling: the client sends GET `/messages?since=100` and the server holds the response open until either a new message arrives or a timeout (30s) expires; the server then responds and the client immediately re-requests. Median latency is the time from message arrival to the next parked poll being woken — typically 50-500 ms — because the server responds the instant data is available. Overhead is one HTTP request per cycle, but cycles are 30s long when idle, so 1M users × 1 req/30s = 33k req/s of overhead — 6x less than short polling. Both are still HTTP request-response; long polling just delays the response to fake push. Real-world: Gmail Chat (2005) used long polling; many status-page widgets still use short polling because simplicity beats latency.
**Visual:**
```
short poll (5s interval):
  client --GET--> server --[]--> client (wait 5s) --GET--> server --[msg]--> client
  median latency: 2.5s; 1 req per 5s per user always

long poll (30s timeout):
  client --GET--> server (hold) --[msg]--> client --GET--> server (hold)...
  median latency: ~200ms (instant on msg arrival); 1 req per 30s when idle
```

### Q2. Why did long polling drive the industry toward async servers?
**Answer:** A thread-per-request server (Apache prefork MPM, older Tomcat, Flask dev server, Django runserver) assigns one OS thread to each in-flight HTTP request. If the request takes 30s to respond (because it's parked waiting for a message), that thread is blocked for 30s doing nothing. OS threads are expensive: ~1-8 MB of stack each, ~10-100 microseconds to context-switch, hard limit of a few thousand per process. At 10k concurrent parked long polls you've consumed 10-40 GB of stack memory and you've hit thread limits, with the threads doing zero useful work. Async frameworks (Node.js event loop, Python asyncio, Go goroutines, Java Netty, Erlang processes) park the request as a Future/Promise/callback that consumes a few KB of memory and no thread; the underlying worker thread is freed to handle other requests. At 10k parked long polls, an async server uses ~50 MB of memory for the parked futures and 4-8 worker threads total. This is why Node.js, Twisted, Tornado, and later asyncio became the dominant platforms for real-time web in the long-polling era — Facebook's chat subsystem was written in Erlang precisely because Erlang's lightweight processes made millions of parked connections feasible. The async transition was forced by long polling; WebSockets and SSE reinforced it because they have the same "many idle connections" characteristic.
**Visual:**
```
thread-per-request (Apache prefork, Flask dev):
  10k parked polls = 10k OS threads = 10-80 GB stack, hit thread limit
  threads idle, doing nothing, just holding the request open

async (Node, asyncio, Go, Erlang):
  10k parked polls = 10k Futures in memory = ~50 MB total
  4-8 worker threads handle all 10k via event loop
  idle polls cost nothing but a few KB each
```

### Q3. How do you avoid losing or duplicating messages between poll cycles?
**Answer:** The classic bug: client polls and gets msg id=100; client re-requests `?since=100`; meanwhile msg id=101 is published in the gap between the response and the next request — does the client miss it? The fix is server-side cursor semantics: every message has a monotonically increasing id (per user or per channel), and the server returns ALL messages with id > `since`, not just "messages that arrived after the poll started". So if msg 101 was published between cycles, the next poll `?since=100` returns it immediately. The server must persist messages in a durable queue (not just in-memory on the parked future) so they survive a cycle gap or even a server restart. To avoid duplicates, the client tracks the highest id it has durably processed (persisted to localStorage or acknowledged to the server) and uses that as the next `since`; if the client crashes mid-processing and re-requests `?since=100` after already processing 101, the server re-delivers 101 and the client deduplicates by id (idempotent processing). For at-most-once semantics on the publish side, the publisher includes a client-generated idempotency key; the server deduplicates on insert. WhatsApp, Slack, and Discord all use this pattern: monotonically increasing seq numbers per conversation, server-side queue with seq-based replay on reconnect, client dedup by seq. The same pattern applies to Kafka consumer offsets (Phase 6) — `since` is exactly an offset.
**Visual:**
```
client polls since=100, gets msg 100, processes it
client re-requests since=100 (last successful id)
  server returns ALL msg id > 100 (i.e., 101, 102 if both arrived in gap)

server-side queue (durable):
  user_inbox: [msg 100, msg 101, msg 102]
  poll(since=100) -> [101, 102]   (never lost)

client crash mid-process of msg 101:
  on restart, polls since=100 again
  server re-delivers [101, 102]
  client dedup by id (idempotent)
```

### Q4. What is the difference between long polling and SSE?
**Answer:** Both deliver server push over plain HTTP, but the mechanics differ. **Long polling**: client GETs `/poll?since=N`; server holds the response open; when data is ready, server writes the body (typically JSON) and closes the response; client immediately re-GETs. Each "push" is one full HTTP request-response cycle with all headers repeated. **SSE**: client opens a single long-lived GET to `/stream`; the server keeps the response open forever and writes `data: ...\n\n` chunks as events arrive; the client reads them as a stream; the connection is one HTTP request that never closes (until the server or client ends it). Differences: (1) **Overhead** — long polling repeats all HTTP headers on every cycle (200-800 bytes per cycle); SSE has one set of headers for the lifetime of the connection. (2) **Latency** — long polling has a one-RTT gap between cycles (client receives response, processes, sends next request); SSE has no gap (server pushes immediately). (3) **Browser API** — long polling uses XHR/fetch (manual loop); SSE uses the native `EventSource` API with auto-reconnect and `Last-Event-ID`. (4) **Bidirectional** — neither is bidirectional; both require a separate POST for client-to-server. (5) **Connection limit** — long polling burns one of the browser's 6 per-origin connections per cycle; SSE uses one for the lifetime. SSE is strictly better for server-to-client push; long polling is the fallback when proxies buffer SSE responses. ChatGPT token streaming, Twitter live feed, and GitHub live actions all use SSE; legacy systems like Gmail Chat (2005) used long polling because SSE didn't exist yet.
**Visual:**
```
long polling:    GET /poll?since=100  -> 200 OK [msgs]  -> GET /poll?since=101 -> ...
                (full HTTP cycle per push, headers repeated each time)

SSE:             GET /stream  -> 200 OK (kept open)
                                  data: msg1\n\n
                                  data: msg2\n\n
                                  data: msg3\n\n   (server pushes chunks)
                (one HTTP request, no headers repeated, no cycle gap)
```

### Q5. Why does long polling have worse tail latency than WebSockets?
**Answer:** Long polling's median latency is excellent (50-500 ms — the time from message arrival to the parked poll being woken), but the p99 tail is worse than WebSockets for several reasons. (1) **Cycle gap** — when a poll cycle ends (server responds with messages), the client must process the response and issue the next GET; during this 50-200 ms gap, no poll is parked, so any message that arrives in this window waits at the server until the next cycle starts, adding up to 200 ms of latency. WebSockets have no cycle gap — the connection is always open, push is immediate. (2) **Timeout coincidence** — if a message arrives at t=30.001s and the server's poll timeout is 30s, the server has just sent an empty response; the message waits for the client to re-request, adding 50-200 ms. (3) **HTTP overhead** — every cycle re-sends cookies, auth tokens, and TLS handshake (if not keep-alive); on mobile networks with high RTT, this adds 100-500 ms per cycle. (4) **Proxy buffering** — some proxies buffer the response body until the connection closes, defeating long polling; the workaround is to chunk-encode and flush, but proxies can still delay. (5) **Connection reuse** — long polling typically uses HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, but if the connection is dropped between cycles (proxy idle timeout), the client must re-establish TLS, adding 200-1000 ms. WebSockets avoid all of these by being one persistent full-duplex connection. For p99 latency-sensitive apps (chat, trading), WebSockets win; for simple push where p99 is acceptable, SSE or long polling is fine.
**Visual:**
```
long polling p99 latency sources:
  cycle gap       50-200 ms  (no poll parked between cycles)
  timeout coinc.  50-200 ms  (msg arrives just after timeout)
  HTTP overhead   100-500 ms (mobile TLS handshake if keep-alive dropped)
  proxy buffering 0-5000 ms  (if proxy holds response until close)

WebSocket p99 latency sources:
  none of the above — single persistent connection, instant push

=> WebSocket p99 ~ 50-100 ms; long poll p99 ~ 200-1000 ms on mobile
```

### Q6. When would you choose long polling over SSE or WebSockets?
**Answer:** Choose long polling when: (1) **You must support legacy proxies** that buffer SSE streams or strip WebSocket Upgrade headers — long polling uses normal HTTP responses that complete and close, so even proxies that buffer until close work (with the trade-off of higher latency). (2) **You need bidirectional communication but cannot use WebSockets** — long polling for server-to-client plus a normal POST for client-to-server is the universal fallback pattern (Slack, Discord, WhatsApp all ship this as a fallback). (3) **Your server framework is async-challenged** — if you're stuck on a thread-per-request server (older Django, Flask without async), you can implement long polling with a thread pool of bounded size, while SSE requires streaming responses that older WSGI servers may not support. (4) **You need simple load balancing** — long polling requests are short-lived (one cycle each), so any L7 LB works; WebSockets require sticky sessions, and SSE benefits from sticky sessions too (to keep one connection on one server). (5) **You're serving a tiny number of users** — for an internal admin dashboard with 5 users, the simplicity of long polling outweighs the marginal latency improvement of SSE/WebSockets. Otherwise, prefer SSE for server-to-client push (simpler, less overhead, native browser API) and WebSockets for bidirectional (chat, multiplayer). Long polling is the right answer to "what do you do when WebSockets and SSE both fail" — it's the universal fallback.
**Visual:**
```
decision tree:
  bidirectional (chat, multiplayer)?       -> WebSocket
  server->client only (live feed, notifs)? -> SSE
  WebSockets and SSE both blocked?         -> long polling (fallback)
  thread-per-request server, can't stream? -> long polling
  tiny user base, simplicity matters?      -> long polling
```

### Q7. How do you handle reconnect and backoff in a long-polling client?
**Answer:** A robust long-polling client must handle three failure modes: (1) the server returns an error (5xx, 429), (2) the connection drops mid-poll (proxy timeout, network change), (3) the client itself crashes and restarts. The recipe: (1) **Exponential backoff with jitter** — on failure, wait 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s, capped at 30s, with ±20% jitter to avoid thundering herd when the server recovers; reset to 1s on the first successful poll. (2) **Retry-After header** — if the server returns 429 or 503 with `Retry-After: 30`, honor it instead of using the backoff schedule. (3) **Last-seen cursor persistence** — the client persists `last_id` to localStorage (web) or SQLite (mobile) on every successful poll, so a restart resumes from the right point without re-receiving old messages. (4) **Heartbeat on idle** — if the server's poll timeout is 30s and the client sees no response for 60s, assume the connection is dead, abort the request, and re-poll. (5) **Visibility change handling** — when the browser tab is hidden, throttle polls to every 60s to save battery; when visible again, immediately poll to catch up. (6) **Online/offline events** — listen to `window.online` to immediately re-poll when the network returns after a dropout. WhatsApp, Slack, and Discord all implement this pattern in their long-poll fallbacks. The general principle: never assume the network is reliable; always have a backoff strategy, always persist your cursor, always handle the crash-and-restart case.
**Visual:**
```
poll ok    -> backoff reset to 1s, persist last_id, next poll immediately
poll 5xx   -> backoff 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s, 30s (jitter ±20%)
poll 429   -> honor Retry-After header
conn drop  -> abort, exponential backoff
tab hidden -> throttle to 60s polls
tab shown  -> immediate poll to catch up
restart    -> read last_id from localStorage, resume
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You are designing Gmail Chat in 2005. WebSockets don't exist. How do you deliver messages in real time?
**Answer:** This is literally the problem long polling was invented to solve. The architecture: (1) **Client** opens a long-poll GET to `/messages?since=<last_id>` on page load; the server parks the request. (2) **Server** is a custom async subsystem (Erlang in Facebook's case; C++ with libevent in Gmail's case) that holds millions of parked requests efficiently as in-memory futures, not OS threads. (3) **Publish path** — when user A sends a message to user B via POST `/send`, the server looks up B's parked poll (by user_id -> future map), resolves it with the new message, and B's poll returns immediately. (4) **Inbox durability** — messages are also persisted to B's inbox in MySQL (or a sharded key-value store) so if B is offline, the message is delivered on B's next poll. (5) **Cycle gap mitigation** — the client immediately re-polls after receiving a response; the gap is 50-200 ms which is acceptable for chat. (6) **Connection limit** — browsers allowed 2 connections per origin in 2005 (HTTP/1.1 spec); one was used for the long poll, the other for POSTing sends and loading assets. (7) **Fallback** — if the long poll fails (proxy timeout), fall back to short polling every 5s. (8) **Timeout** — server responds with empty 200 after 30s to keep proxies from killing the connection. The result: sub-second median delivery latency, working in every browser, no plugins, no proprietary protocol. This was state of the art until WebSockets standardized in 2011.
**Visual:**
```
alice's browser                          server                          bob's browser
  |  GET /poll?since=100                                                  |
  |--------------------------------------->| (parked, async)              |
  |                                        |                              |
  |                                  POST /send to=bob text="hi"          |
  |<-----------------------------------------------------------------------|
  |                                        | resolve bob's parked future  |
  |                                        | (lookup user_id -> future)   |
  |  200 OK [{id:101, text:"hi"}]          |                              |
  |<---------------------------------------|                              |
  |  GET /poll?since=101                   |                              |
  |--------------------------------------->| (park again)                 |
```

### Q2. Your long-polling server runs on Flask (synchronous, thread-per-request). It works at 100 users but dies at 1000. Why, and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** Flask's default dev server (`app.run()`) is single-threaded and synchronous — it processes one request at a time. With long polling, the first request parks for up to 30 seconds; during that time, no other request can be served. 100 users means 100 parked requests; if the server is single-threaded, 99 of them are queued, and the apparent latency is 30s × 99 = ~50 minutes per request. Even with `app.run(threaded=True)` (which spawns an OS thread per request), 1000 parked long polls = 1000 OS threads = 4-8 GB of stack memory and thread-limit exhaustion. The fix has three levels. (1) **Switch to an async framework** — move from Flask to Quart (async Flask), FastAPI + asyncio, or aiohttp. Async frameworks park requests as futures (a few KB each) instead of OS threads (1-8 MB each), so 10k parked polls use ~50 MB instead of 10 GB. (2) **Use a proper WSGI/ASGI server** — gunicorn with `worker_class=uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker` for ASGI, or gunicorn with many sync workers if you must stay on WSGI (each worker can hold one request, so 16 workers = 16 concurrent parked polls — not great). (3) **If you must stay on Flask**, use a background task queue — the long-poll endpoint quickly checks for messages, and if none, returns a 202 with a `Retry-After: 2` header telling the client to short-poll every 2s; this degrades to short polling but at least doesn't park threads. The real fix is always "move to async". This is exactly why the long-polling era drove the adoption of Node.js, Tornado, Twisted, and later asyncio — they were the only way to hold many idle connections cheaply.
**Visual:**
```
Flask dev (single-threaded):   1 parked poll blocks all others (broken)
Flask threaded:                1000 parked polls = 1000 OS threads (OOM)
Flask + gunicorn sync workers: 16 workers = 16 concurrent polls (still bad)

Fix:
  Flask -> Quart (async drop-in)             -> 10k polls = 50 MB
  Flask -> FastAPI + asyncio                 -> 10k polls = 50 MB
  Flask -> aiohttp                           -> 10k polls = 50 MB
  (async framework: park as future, not thread)
```

### Q3. Your long-polling server has a p99 latency of 5 seconds but p50 is 100 ms. Diagnose.
**Answer:** A bimodal latency distribution (good p50, terrible p99) in a long-polling system points to specific failure modes. (1) **Cycle gap effect** — p50 hits users whose poll happened to be parked when the message arrived (instant delivery); p99 hits users whose message arrived just after their previous poll returned and they're in the 50-200 ms cycle gap. But a 5-second p99 is too high for cycle gap alone. (2) **Proxy idle timeout** — some corporate proxies kill idle connections at 30 or 60 seconds, but if the server's poll timeout is 30s, the connection is never idle for 30s, so this is unlikely the cause. (3) **Server-side queue saturation** — the publish path fans out to N parked polls; if N is large (e.g., a group chat with 10k recipients) and the fan-out is single-threaded, the last recipient in the loop gets the message seconds after the first. Fix: parallelize the fan-out across worker threads or use a pub/sub system. (4) **Database hotspot on publish** — every publish writes to the inbox; if the DB is the bottleneck (e.g., 1000 publishes/sec hitting a single MySQL row), publishes queue up and the parked polls wait. Fix: shard the inbox, use a write-optimized store (Cassandra, ScyllaDB), or buffer writes. (5) **GC pauses** — Java/Go servers with large heaps can pause for seconds during GC, during which all parked polls are frozen. Fix: tune GC, use generational collectors, or move to a runtime with predictable pauses (Erlang, Rust). (6) **Network jitter on mobile** — mobile RTT can spike to seconds on handoff between cell towers; the cycle gap compounds this. Fix: WebSockets or SSE would reduce cycles and thus reduce the impact of network jitter. Diagnose by: instrument publish-to-deliver latency (server-side timestamp on publish, client echoes it back on ack), group by recipient cohort, and find which cohort has the bad p99.
**Visual:**
```
p50 = 100ms   (parked poll, instant wake on publish)
p99 = 5s      (something delayed the wake)

hypotheses:
  cycle gap            50-200ms     (too small to explain 5s)
  proxy timeout        30s+         (too large)
  fan-out single-thr   O(N)         (plausible for big groups)
  DB hotspot           queueing     (plausible at high QPS)
  GC pause             1-5s         (plausible for Java/Go)
  mobile handoff       1-5s         (plausible for mobile users)

instrument: publish_ts (server) -> deliver_ts (client ack) -> p99 by cohort
```

### Q4. You are migrating Gmail Chat from long polling to WebSockets in 2012. What changes, and what stays the same?
**Answer:** What changes: (1) **Transport** — the client opens a WebSocket instead of issuing a long-poll GET; the server holds a WebSocket connection per user instead of a parked HTTP request. (2) **Per-message overhead** — drops from 200-800 bytes (HTTP headers per cycle) to 2-14 bytes (WebSocket frame header). At 1M users × 1 msg/sec, that's megabytes/sec of bandwidth saved. (3) **Latency** — cycle gap disappears; p99 drops from 200-1000 ms to 50-100 ms. (4) **Bidirectional** — client can send messages over the same socket (no separate POST), simplifying the protocol. (5) **Server framework** — async is still required (WebSockets have the same "many idle connections" characteristic as long polling), but the framework must support WebSocket frames natively. (6) **Load balancing** — must switch from stateless L7 LB (any request to any backend) to sticky sessions (a reconnecting client must land on the same backend holding its socket state). What stays the same: (1) **Server-side message queue per user** — still needed for offline delivery and for replay on reconnect. (2) **Sequence numbers and cursors** — still needed to resume after a dropped connection. (3) **Publish fan-out** — the same pub/sub pattern (publish to user X, the server holding X's connection delivers). (4) **Heartbeats** — ping/pong replaces the long-poll timeout but serves the same purpose (detect dead connections). (5) **Fallback** — long polling remains the fallback for clients whose proxies block WebSockets. The migration is essentially "swap the transport, keep the application-layer delivery semantics"; the hard parts (durability, ordering, fan-out, reconnection) are unchanged.
**Visual:**
```
before (long poll):
  client <--GET /poll?since=N--> server  (HTTP cycle per push)
  client --POST /send--> server          (separate cycle for sends)

after (WebSocket):
  client <--ws frame--> server           (one persistent connection)
  (push + send on same socket)

unchanged:
  server-side per-user queue
  monotonic seq numbers
  publish fan-out (pub/sub)
  heartbeat (ping/pong replaces timeout)
  long-poll fallback for blocked clients
```

### Q5. Your long-polling server is being DDoSed — attackers open millions of polls and never close them. How do you defend?
**Answer:** A long-polling server is particularly vulnerable to resource-exhaustion DoS because each parked request consumes memory and a slot in the connection table, even if it's "idle". Defense layers: (1) **Rate limit per IP** — allow at most N (say 5) concurrent parked polls per source IP; reject additional with 429 Too Many Requests. (2) **Authentication required** — require a valid session token to poll; unauthenticated requests get 401 immediately, before they can park. (3) **Per-user connection cap** — once a user has one parked poll, reject additional with 409 Conflict (a user should only have one poll in flight). (4) **Aggressive timeout** — cap parked poll duration at 30s (not 5 minutes); if no message arrives, return empty 200 and let the client re-poll. This bounds the maximum time an attacker can hold a slot. (5) **Global connection cap** — once the server has reached its max parked polls (say 1M), reject new polls with 503 Service Unavailable + `Retry-After: 5`; this prevents OOM at the cost of rejecting legitimate users during an attack. (6) **CAPTCHA on login** — make it expensive for attackers to obtain session tokens; bot-driven attacks must solve CAPTCHAs. (7) **CDN/WAF** — Cloudflare or AWS WAF in front to absorb volumetric attacks, rate-limit by IP, and challenge suspicious traffic. (8) **Sharded architecture** — distribute parked polls across many gateway shards; an attack on one shard doesn't take down the others. (9) **Auto-scale** — if parked polls grow abnormally fast, auto-scale the gateway fleet; cloud providers can add capacity in 30-60 seconds. Real-world: Slack, Discord, and WhatsApp all combine these — auth required, per-user one-poll cap, 30s timeout, Cloudflare in front, and auto-scaling.
**Visual:**
```
attack: 1M bots open long polls, never close

defense layers:
  1. Cloudflare WAF (absorb volumetric, challenge suspicious)
  2. Auth required (401 if no session token)
  3. Per-IP rate limit (5 concurrent polls max)
  4. Per-user one-poll cap (409 if second poll)
  5. 30s max park time (bounds slot hold)
  6. Global cap (503 Retry-After:5 if total > 1M)
  7. Auto-scale gateway fleet if parked polls spike
```

### Q6. You need to push live stock prices to 100k browser clients. Long polling, SSE, or WebSockets?
**Answer:** For server-to-client push of stock prices to 100k browsers, **SSE is the right answer**, not long polling and not WebSockets. Reasoning: (1) **Direction** — stock prices are pure server-to-client; the client doesn't send data back (other than an occasional subscription change, which can be a separate POST). WebSockets' bidirectional capability is wasted here. (2) **Browser API** — `EventSource` is native, auto-reconnects with `Last-Event-ID`, and handles backpressure gracefully. Long polling requires a manual XHR loop with custom reconnection logic. (3) **Overhead** — SSE has one HTTP request per connection for its lifetime; long polling has one per cycle (every 30s or every price update). At 1 update/second per stock × 100k clients, long polling would generate 100k req/sec of pure HTTP overhead; SSE generates 0 (the connection is already open). (4) **Proxy compatibility** — SSE works through most modern proxies; long polling works through all proxies (even legacy ones). If your audience includes corporate users behind very old proxies, you might need a long-polling fallback. (5) **Multiplexing** — HTTP/2 lets multiple SSE streams share one TCP connection, further reducing overhead. (6) **Why not WebSockets?** — WebSockets would work fine, but they add complexity (sticky sessions, manual reconnection, custom backpressure) for no benefit when the traffic is one-way. Bloomberg's web terminal, Twitter's live feed, and ChatGPT's token streaming all use SSE for exactly this reason. The decision tree: bidirectional → WebSocket; server-to-client only → SSE; SSE blocked → long polling fallback.
**Visual:**
```
100k clients, 1 push/sec each
  long polling: 100k req/sec of HTTP overhead (headers per cycle)
  SSE:          0 req/sec overhead (one connection per client, lifetime)
  WebSocket:    0 req/sec overhead, but sticky sessions + manual reconnect

SSE wins for pure server->client push
  - native EventSource API with auto-reconnect
  - one HTTP request per connection lifetime
  - HTTP/2 multiplexing
  - simpler than WebSockets for one-way traffic
```

### Q7. Your mobile app uses long polling and burns through users' battery. Why, and what do you do?
**Answer:** Mobile battery drain from long polling comes from two sources: (1) **Radio wakeups** — every HTTP request wakes the cellular radio, which stays in high-power mode for 5-10 seconds after the last packet before dropping to idle. At one poll cycle per 30s, the radio is essentially always in high-power mode, draining battery at 100-300 mA instead of 5-10 mA idle. (2) **TLS handshakes** — if the keep-alive connection drops (mobile networks drop idle connections aggressively), every cycle re-establishes TLS, which is 1-2 seconds of CPU + radio time. Mitigations: (1) **Switch to platform push** — use Apple Push Notification Service (APNs) for iOS and Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) for Android; these maintain a single system-level persistent connection to Apple/Google's servers, which is shared across all apps on the device. Your server pushes to APNs/FCM, they push to the device over the system connection, the radio wakes only for actual notifications. This is what WhatsApp, Slack, and Instagram all do for offline push. (2) **Use WebSockets for foreground, APNs/FCM for background** — when the app is open, a WebSocket keeps latency low; when the app is backgrounded, close the WebSocket and rely on APNs/FCM for delivery. (3) **Adaptive poll interval** — when the app is in the foreground, poll every 30s; when backgrounded, drop to every 5 minutes or close the connection entirely and use APNs/FCM. (4) **Coalesce notifications** — if multiple notifications are pending on the server, send them as one batch in one response, not as separate polls. (5) **Longer server timeout** — if you must poll, push the server timeout to 60-90s (mobile networks tolerate longer idles than corporate proxies), reducing the number of cycles per hour. The real fix is almost always "use APNs/FCM for background, WebSocket for foreground, abandon long polling for mobile".
**Visual:**
```
mobile long polling:
  radio wakes every 30s for HTTP cycle, stays high-power 5-10s after
  => radio essentially never sleeps => 100-300 mA drain => battery dies in 4h

better:
  foreground: WebSocket (one persistent connection, low overhead)
  background: APNs (iOS) / FCM (Android) - system-level shared connection
              radio wakes ONLY for actual notifications
  adaptive:   foreground=ws, backgrounded=close ws + use APNs/FCM
  coalesce:   batch multiple notifications into one push
```

quiz.explanation: Short polling: the client sends GET /messages every N seconds (say 5s); the server responds immediately with whatever is queued (possibly empty); the client waits 5s and asks again. Median latency to receive a new message is N/2 (2.5s on average for a 5s poll), and the client burns one HTTP request every N seconds even when nothing is happening — at 1M users × 1 req/5s = 200k requests/second of pure overhead.

quiz.explanation: A thread-per-request server (Apache prefork MPM, older Tomcat, Flask dev server, Django runserver) assigns one OS thread to each in-flight HTTP request. If the request takes 30s to respond (because it's parked waiting for a message), that thread is blocked for 30s doing nothing. OS threads are expensive: ~1-8 MB of stack each, ~10-100 microseconds to context-switch, hard limit of a few thousand per process.
